title: Heterogeneous GPU Rollout and Emergency Capacity Plan (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is an operational runbook draft for handling infra incidents that require: replacing GPUs in heterogeneous clusters, cordon/drain workflows when hardware degrades, injecting capacity quickly with mixed-instance pools, and safe rollback to degraded-mode model variants.

Scope / When to use this doc:
- GPU hardware failures that affect model-serving pods (kernel faults, ECC, NVLINK errors)
- Node-level GPU health alerts flagged by nvml / node-exporter or telemetry (GPU-err > threshold)
- Capacity shortfalls triggered by surge or zone outage where we need fast, controlled capacity add from a secondary pool or pre-warmed bridge nodes
- Emergency replacement where physical replacement of cards is required and we must avoid mass eviction and client-impact spikes

Key principles:
- Prefer minimizing live-pod disruption: use node-label / taint strategies to redirect new scheduling rather than bulk eviction when possible
- Fallback first: route traffic to smaller/quantized model variants before mass draining hardware
- Clear, timeboxed steps and owner for each phase; avoid ad-hoc fixes during high-severity without a paired reviewer

Quick triage checklist (first 15 mins):
1) Confirm alert: check Grafana panel "gpu-health-summary" and the node alert in PagerDuty ticket.
2) Identify scope: single GPU on node (partial) vs. node-level multi-GPU failure vs. zone-wide GPU flapping.
3) Run nvml check: ssh to node (if accessible) and run: sudo python3 /opt/sre/bin/gpu_health_check.py --short
   - If nvml returns ECC or persistent faults -> treat as hardware, proceed to cordon and notify hardware team.
4) If node unreachable: check console / IPMI / cloud instance status and open a parallel infra-ops Jira.
5) Post an incident note in slack:#infra-oncall with initial assessment and ETA for next update.

Immediate mitigation (0–30 mins):
- If single GPU failing but node still functional:
  a) Label node: kubectl label node NODENAME gpu-degraded=true --overwrite
  b) Add taint to discourage scheduling: kubectl taint nodes NODENAME gpu-degraded=true:NoSchedule --overwrite
  c) Update Kuma/edge-router routing policy if this node backs specific customer routes (temporary redirect to pool_2).
  d) Trigger a controlled restart for affected pods only if they show OOM or GPU allocation failures: kubectl rollout restart deploy/NAME -n model-serving
- If node has multi-GPU faults or kernel panic:
  a) Cordon node: kubectl cordon NODENAME
  b) Drain with grace but keep critical system pods: kubectl drain NODENAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --pod-selector='app!=infra-monitoring' --grace-period=120
  c) If drain blocks > 5 mins, move to forced eviction for the smallest set to recover capacity: kubectl delete pod PODNAME -n model-serving --grace-period=5 --force

Hardware replacement path (if physical swap required):
- Owner: oncall + infra-hardware engineer (assign in Jira).
- Preflight: ensure the replacement GPU SKU and firmware rev are compatible with node-pool label. If heterogeneous SKUs are allowed, annotate the node: kubectl annotate node NODENAME gpu-sku=H100-80gb-hybrid
- Hot-swap steps (data-center or remote tech):
  1) Power down node following safe shutdown playbook (link in Confluence).
  2) Remove faulty accelerator and install replacement. Log serial number in Jira ticket.
  3) Boot node and verify nvml lists expected devices: nvidia-smi -q | grep "Product Name"
  4) Run extended gpu_health_check: sudo python3 /opt/sre/bin/gpu_health_check.py --full | tee /var/log/gpu_post_swap.log
  5) Remove taint/label and uncordon: kubectl label node NODENAME gpu-degraded- || true; kubectl taint nodes NODENAME gpu-degraded:NoSchedule- || true; kubectl uncordon NODENAME
  6) Rebalance pods if needed: kubectl rollout restart daemonset/model-affinity -n model-serving (only if verified stable)

Heterogeneous rollout considerations (mixing A100/H100/L4):
- If a node joins with different SKU, ensure admission controls and model affinity tolerations are set. Avoid scheduling highest-memory models on smaller GPUs via resource-class constraints.
- Use node-pool labels: gpu.family=A100 or gpu.family=L4 and set deployment nodeSelectors accordingly for heavyweight models.
- When adding capacity from mixed pools, validate latency/throughput on a small canary before routing production traffic.

Rapid capacity injection (burst pool / bridge nodes):
- When cluster utilization > 85% and autoscaler cannot meet demand within SLA, trigger capacity injection from pre-warmed burst pool (named pool-burst-1). Steps:
  1) Run terraform apply -var='scale_to=+5' -target=module.burst_pool (ops-runner account) — confirm instance creation in cloud console.
  2) Label new nodes with "prewarmed=true" and set taints to accept only canary deployments: kubectl label node NODENAME prewarmed=true; kubectl taint nodes NODENAME prewarmed=true:PreferNoSchedule
  3) Deploy a canary model instance (small traffic slice) to validate perf: kubectl apply -f canary/hetero-burst-canary.yaml -n model-serving
  4) Monitor tail-latency panels for 10m; if stable, remove PreferNoSchedule taint and add them to routing pool.
- Note: if prewarmed pool uses cheaper GPU class (e.g., L4), reduce batch size and enable caching to avoid latency regressions. Use Optimize recommendations tag: "burst-auto-downscale-quant".

Routing and client safety (to avoid 429/timeout storms):
- Before large drain/unavailable event, enable per-customer throttles in Kong/API-GW to avoid retry storms (set retry: 0, rate-limit: 50r/s per token).
- Flip a runtime flag to route to quantized variant: curl -X POST $RUNTIME_API/flags -d '{"name":"force_quant_route","value":true}' (ops token required).
- Short-circuit large-batch jobs to offline queue (Celery: set priority=low)

Rollback and degraded-mode operations:
- If GPU swap/uncordon causes regression in correctness or latency > SLO:
  1) Re-cordon the node: kubectl cordon NODENAME
  2) Scale down new nodes (terraform plan -> apply to remove) and route back to previous pool.
  3) Re-enable previous model variant routing flag.
  4) Open postmortem action item and freeze releases to model-serving until RCA is complete.

Post-incident checklist (during recovery / 24–72hrs):
- Complete hardware ticket: record serial numbers, replacement vendor, RMA info.
- Upload gpu_post_swap.log to Jira and Confluence incident page.
- Run regression eval against golden prompt-set (runbooks/ci/evals/hetero-gpu-regress.yaml).
- Update the telemetry thresholds if noise caused false positive alerts.
- If capacity injection incurred extra spend, coordinate finance tagging for chargeback and notify finance ops.

Open questions / TODOs (items to convert to permanent runbook steps):
- Define exact TTLs for prewarmed node taints and automatic scale-down policy (currently manual).
- Add a training script to exercise mixed-GPU scheduling in staging to catch performance cliffs earlier.
- Formalize compatibility matrix for allowed firmware versions across mixed SKU clusters.

Appendix: useful commands and probes
- GPU quick status: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total,memory.used,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv,noheader -i 0
- NVML python health script: sudo python3 /opt/sre/bin/gpu_health_check.py --full --upload-to-s3 s3://infra-logs/gpu_checks/$NODE-$(date +%s).log
- Drain example (safe): kubectl drain NODENAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='app!=infra-monitoring' --grace-period=120
- Forced delete (last resort): kubectl delete pod PODNAME -n model-serving --grace-period=0 --force

Owner / revision history:
- Draft owner: Ethan Morales (eng-sre)
- Contributors: Priya Nair (infra-hw), Liam Ortega (serving-runtime), Yara Singh (observability)
- Draft created: 2025-02-12
- Last edited: 2025-03-01

Notes to self: keep this doc intentionally concise; link to full hardware SOPs rather than duplicate. Run a tabletop next week with dev-product and infra-hw to validate the mixed-GPU path.

End of draft.
